answers.text:
"Superposition" is Anthropic's term of art for a specific strategy neural networks use to represent more features than they have neurons for, by storing multiple features as overlapping (non-orthogonal) directions in the same set of neurons rather than giving each feature its own dedicated neuron. A neuron participating in superposition becomes "polysemantic" — it fires for several unrelated features rather than one — and the price is that you generally can't isolate a single feature with a simple linear probe on activations; recovering it requires a nonlinearity, as the article notes when it says that with superposition "if there's no composition, one can instead store \(\exp(m)\) items in superposition, although a non-linearity is required to retrieve them."

As you may know, this is the concept Chris Olah and colleagues developed at length in Anthropic's earlier paper "Toy Models of Superposition," which this note explicitly builds on: "Since publishing our original paper on superposition, we've had more time to reflect on the relationship between the topics and discuss it with people, and wanted to expand on our earlier discussion in the related work section and share a few thoughts." That earlier paper argued superposition tends to emerge when features are sparse (rarely co-occurring), letting the network exploit unused combinatorial "space" to pack in extra features at the cost of clean linear readability.

In this note specifically, superposition is being set up as one of two things people conflate under the umbrella "distributed representations" — the other being "composition," where independent features combine cleanly and remain linearly separable. The rest of the piece argues these two strategies trade off against each other, and that keeping them conceptually distinct matters for interpretability: composed representations can be understood as a manageable, linear set of features, while superposed ones pack in exponentially more but resist that kind of decomposition.

answers.asked: An informal note on the relationship between superposition and distributed representations by Chris Olah.
answers.text:
This is the byline/description for the piece itself, appearing right under the title. It tells you two things worth noting: who wrote it, and what kind of document it is.

Chris Olah is a researcher known for work on mechanistic interpretability of neural networks; he's associated with Anthropic's interpretability team (the piece is hosted on the "Transformer Circuits Thread," which is Anthropic's venue for this line of research) and was previously known for visualization/interpretability work at OpenAI and Google Brain/DeepMind. The "superposition" concept referenced here comes from earlier work on the "Toy Models of Superposition" paper, which this note explicitly builds on and discusses.

The word "informal" is doing real work, and the piece later cashes it out explicitly: Informal notes allow us to publish ideas that aren't as refined and developed as a full paper, and mistakes are very possible, so it should be treated more like a colleague's shared thoughts or a blog post than a peer-reviewed paper. So the framing here is setting expectations — this is a working reflection rather than a polished, fully defended result, which matches the origin story given just below: distributed representations are a classic idea in both neuroscience and connectionist approaches to AI, and after publishing the original superposition paper, the authors had more time to reflect and discuss the relationship with people, wanting to expand on the earlier discussion and share a few thoughts.

answers.asked: What does "superposition" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
In this piece, superposition is the strategy of packing more features into a layer than it has neurons, by storing them as directions that overlap rather than giving each one its own neuron — the article notes it is "sometimes called 'dense'" and that a code with only 4 neurons can represent all colored shapes "just as 4 bits can represent 16 numbers" [spya-c2eewa]. The cost is that this only works when the underlying features are sparse: dense, always-co-occurring features force one-feature-per-neuron, while sparse, rarely-combined features leave "holes" in the compositional space that can be filled with other features in superposition, and retrieving them back out requires a non-linearity [spya-qbuyka spya-ajbh7f spya-xcrca8].

Why it matters to the argument: the whole note is built around showing that superposition is not the same thing as the other sense of "distributed representation," composition — where independent features (like color and shape) combine linearly to represent objects [spya-qcd003 spya-xcdtte]. The article's central claim is that these two are "fundamentally competing as strategies" for using the same exponential volume of possible states: fully composable features can only fill \(m\) bits with \(m\) features, whereas without composition you can store \(\exp(m)\) items via superposition [spya-xcrca8 spya-jzkekc]. That trade-off is why the piece insists on separating the two ideas rather than treating "distributed" as one spectrum: composition gives you non-local generalization and easy linear interpretability, while superposition gives you more storage but sacrifices exactly that linear readability — "sometimes distributed representations are described as providing both the benefits of non-local generalization and representing more features than neurons, but these properties seem to actually trade-off" [spya-sq6424 spya-armg2f]. Since the goal of interpretability work is to decompose a network's representations into independent, understandable components, this distinction is what tells you when that's even possible in principle, which is why the article opens by saying decomposing representations is necessary "to escape the curse of dimensionality and understand neural networks" [spya-nwuh77 spya-v47ca7].

"Monosemantic" here is being used in its literal sense—having one meaning—applied to a neuron: a monosemantic neuron is one that fires for exactly one thing and represents only that.

In this passage, the "local code" gives each (shape, color) pair its own dedicated neuron, so this model is "monosemantic" and doesn't have any superposition. That's the key link: monosemanticity is being defined as the opposite of superposition. A neuron is monosemantic when it corresponds cleanly to one feature or concept; it becomes polysemantic—responding to multiple, unrelated things—when superposition packs more features into it than it has dimensions for, which is exactly the phenomenon this whole note is building toward (you can see the contrast surface again later, in block 39, where the "semi-distributed" code's units are described as "polysemantic, but only respond to a few features").

So selecting this word here is catching the piece's central vocabulary being introduced for the first time: monosemantic/polysemantic is the neuron-level language that parallels composition/superposition at the representation level, and the local code is the baseline case—maximally interpretable, maximally wasteful—against which everything else in the article (semi-local, dense, semi-distributed codes) will be measured.

answers.asked: In our language, this model is "monosemantic" and doesn't have any superposition.
answers.text:
"Monosemantic" is the article's term for a neuron that represents exactly one thing — here, one specific (shape, color) pair, like "red circle" and nothing else. A neuron is monosemantic when it fires for a single, clean feature rather than being reused to encode several unrelated things.

"Superposition" is the contrasting phenomenon: a network representing more features than it has neurons by having neurons respond to multiple, often unrelated features (making them "polysemantic"), relying on the features being sparse enough that this doesn't cause too much interference. Since the local code in this example gives every distinct (shape, color) combination its own dedicated neuron, there's no need for any neuron to double up — each one does one job, so there's no superposition at all.

This sentence is setting the baseline case for the whole piece's argument. The local code sits at one extreme: maximally wasteful in neuron count, but maximally clean in the sense that every neuron means exactly one thing. Everything that follows — the "semi-local"/compositional code, and then the "dense"/superposed code — is defined by contrast with this starting point, where monosemanticity and the absence of superposition go together.

answers.asked: What does "monosemantic" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
In the article, "monosemantic" describes the pure "local code," where each neuron stands for exactly one (shape, color) pair rather than responding to multiple different things: "We'll start with what Thorpe calls a pure "local code". In this setup, there's a neuron for each (shape, color) pair. In our language, this model is "monosemantic" and doesn't have any superposition." [spya-kcjqdw]

So a monosemantic neuron is one with a single, clean meaning — one feature per neuron — as opposed to a "polysemantic" neuron that fires for several unrelated things at once. The article later uses that contrast when describing the semi-distributed code, where units "begin to have some meaning – they're polysemantic, but only respond to a few features" [spya-vw7xv6].

The concept matters to the argument because monosemanticity is the article's marker for the *absence* of superposition. The piece's whole framework hinges on treating "superposition" and "composition" as two distinct axes people conflate under the umbrella term "distributed representations" [spya-fyxmks]. Superposition is defined by neurons packing more features than they have dimensions for, which forces polysemanticity; monosemantic neurons, by contrast, are the baseline "local" case with no superposition, used as the starting point before the article introduces composition (the semi-local code) and then superposition (the dense code) as separate strategies [spya-kcjqdw spya-xcrca8]. My inference is that by anchoring "monosemantic" to the local code at the very start, the article sets up a clear contrast: composition preserves something like monosemantic, interpretable components even as it combines them, while superposition necessarily sacrifices monosemanticity to pack in more features than neurons — which is exactly the trade-off the piece goes on to formalize [spya-armg2f spya-xcrca8].
